title: Knee-Deep in the Big Muddy
text:
In the mid 1970s Barry Staw asked business school students to play a financial executive at a fictional company whose profits had been falling. They read a case history and were told to allocate 10 million dollars of research and development money to one of two divisions, consumer products or industrial products.

Some students made this first choice themselves. Others were told that a previous executive had made it. Then all of them were shown what happened in the following years: in some versions the chosen division recovered, in others it continued to lose money. Finally, each student had to split a new budget of 20 million dollars between the two divisions.

The pattern was clear. Students who had personally chosen a division that then performed badly put the most money into it on the second round, more than students whose choice had worked out and more than those who had inherited a failing choice from someone else. Being responsible for a bad decision made people throw good money after bad, apparently to justify their earlier judgment. His title echoed a Pete Seeger protest song about a captain who keeps marching his men deeper into a river.
lesson: Owning a failing decision makes it harder to see clearly. Set review points in advance, and let someone without a stake judge whether to continue.
source: Staw, B. M. (1976). Knee-deep in the big muddy: A study of escalating commitment to a chosen course of action. Organizational Behavior and Human Performance, 16(1), 27-44.
